title: Norris sparkles in Sao Paulo despite firework mishap
text:
Showing off on the podium after winning the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Lando Norris made his first misstep of an afternoon that had challenged the Formula 1 drivers to their very limits.

Norris jumped off the top step, and tried to do his signature move, where he uncorks the champagne bottle by bashing it into the ground.

Except that, not for the first time, the force of his jump pushed things too far, and he smashed the bottle.

Then, holding up the shattered top to the crowd below, he stepped backwards and inadvertently put the side of his head into the sparkles blowing up from the fireworks on the front of the platform.

Red Bull drivers Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar showed no pity, and proceeded to drench him with the contents of their bottles.

In any case, Norris was fine, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella confirmed shortly afterwards, and the Briton showed no ill effects in his post-race interviews.

It was, he said, "one of the hardest races of the year in terms of focus needed every lap and therefore one of the best".

Norris wins gripping race after Antonelli and Russell errors

Norris brilliant in wet & Verstappen recovery extraordinary - driver ratings

Interlagos did what it often can, and threw everything at the drivers. The race started on a wet track, which dried progressively. There was more rain at the end.

Through it all, Norris was virtually impeccable. He made new world champion Kimi Antonelli look fallible for pretty much the first time all year, and then fended off what at one point was threatening to be one of those days when Verstappen appears to have descended from the Gods.

It says a lot for Norris' performance that it overshadowed Verstappen's drive from 21st on the grid to finish second.

Actually, perhaps the race had also started with a small blemish from the man who has had to hand his title of world champion to Antonelli this year without ever really being able to defend it.

Starting from pole, Norris was relatively slow away, at least compared with the Italian, and Antonelli blasted into a lead that for a while looked as if he would not lose.

But after the Mercedes driver had built an eight-second advantage in the first 13 laps, Norris began to come back at him as the track dried.

Stopping for slick tyres a lap before Antonelli cut a seven-second deficit to nothing, and when three laps later the new champion spun at Turn One under pressure from the old, Norris was promoted into a lead that he never again looked like losing.

"A lot was thrown at everyone on a day like today, but it was probably one of our best races in terms of execution and pit stops, timing of things," Norris said.

"We boxed one lap early on to the slicks. I came out and was right behind him and forced him to push a little bit more, and obviously he went into a mistake and I could capitalise on it.

"So, in terms of always being there where we needed to be, being able to put people under pressure was a very good day for that.

"Also, from my side, just not making any mistakes, which is so easy to do on a day like today. So, great performance from the whole team. Certainly up there with one of the best I've ever had."

For both Norris and McLaren, it was a welcome return to form. They started the year slowly, having fallen behind in development on their 2026 car as they diverted resources to ensure they got their title double over the line last year.

By mid-summer, they had caught up, and Norris took two consecutive wins either side of the summer break, and was unlucky not to get another in Madrid in September.

But then other teams overtook them again and McLaren have toiled relatively in recent races, especially in qualifying.

But the combination in Sao Paulo of some new parts, the circuit characteristics suiting them, and Norris excelling in the wet in qualifying and race, put him back in the game.

In so doing, he provided a performance that served as a reminder that he has been one of the drivers of the year, even if his equipment has not always met his exalted standards.

Stella said: "When Lando operates at his best, he's definitely one of the best drivers on the grid.

"We have seen that in these conditions, like yesterday (in qualifying), it's not the first time that when you have mixed variable conditions, he kind of is one of the fastest in finding the limit.

"And you have seen this today as well, when the track was in the middle between dry and wet. It was when he was probably gaining most throughout the races on anybody else.

"He's very sensitive in understanding how much grip is available. And very, I would say, even complete as a driver, despite he's still many years ahead of him, from a technical point of view, in terms of understanding how to deploy his tools to use the grip that is available, or to adapt to the balance of the car, because you're never going to have a really perfect car.

"You're never going to have the perfect conditions. So adaptability is actually probably the most important feature that you may want to possess as a driver. When there's a need to understand what's best, how to operate, he's definitely a master."

For a time, it looked as if Verstappen might be in the running for a win.

A penalty for using too many engines this year left the four-time champion four places lower than the position from which he had won in similar slippery conditions at Interlagos two years ago.

So when he was up to fifth, and less than 15 seconds behind leader Antonelli, by the time the pit stops for dry tyres were looming on lap 15, with 56 still to go and more rain predicted, it looked ominous.

But once on to the slicks, Verstappen was not a threat to Norris on pace, even when heavy rain returned in the closing laps.

"That first stint went really, really well," Verstappen said. "We got very quickly back into the top 10, and the pace wasn't bad.…

title: Norris wins gripping race after Antonelli and Russell errors
text:
McLaren's Lando Norris beat Max Verstappen to win a gripping Sao Paulo Grand Prix in which new world champion Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes team-mate George Russell both made critical mistakes in difficult conditions.

Norris, who started from pole, lost the lead to Antonelli at the start and dropped back when the track was wet.

But an earlier pit stop for dry-weather tyres put Norris on Antonelli's tail and the Italian spun away the lead at the first corner.

After reclaiming first place, Norris dominated through a late shower of rain which required a switch back to wet-weather tyres to take his first win since the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August.

A few laps before Antonelli lost the lead, Russell, who started seventh, spun exiting the pits and lost 15 to 20 seconds after working his way back into podium contention.

Despite their travails, Russell and Antonelli finished fourth and fifth to clinch the constructors' championship for Mercedes a week after the Italian had tied up the drivers' title.

Norris had too much pace for Verstappen whether the track was dry or wet and stamped his authority on the race.

But the Dutchman put in another supreme drive in changeable conditions in Interlagos to take second after starting in 21st place.

An accomplished performance from Norris in a revived McLaren to take his first win for more than two months

A superb comeback from Verstappen from an engine penalty

A difficult day for both Mercedes, notwithstanding the greater glory of the constructors' win, and Ferrari in the tricky conditions

Norris had started from his first pole position since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, but lost first place immediately after Antonelli, alongside him on the front row, leaped into the lead.

The new world champion pulled away to build a five-second advantage in 10 laps as he began to look as if he might crown his achievement with a win at the first attempt.

Antonelli's lead was more than eight seconds by lap 13 but the track was drying and three laps later Norris came in for dry-weather slick tyres.

The Italian followed him in a lap later, but Norris had gained so much time with his earlier stop that he was on the Mercedes' gearbox when it rejoined.

Antonelli defended for a couple of laps but he was complaining over the radio that the car felt strange under acceleration, and on lap 20 he lost control on the entry to Turn One, spinning and handing the lead to Norris.

That left Norris three seconds ahead of Hadjar with Verstappen now close behind Antonelli, who ran wide again at Turn One four laps later and handed third place to the Dutchman.

Hadjar had every bit as much pace as Verstappen, but was not as consistent and made too many mistakes, and within 10 laps the team leader was on the Frenchman's tail.

Red Bull ordered Hadjar to let Verstappen by on lap 39 in the hope the four-time champion could close on Norris.

But the Briton had too much pace and held off Verstappen, switching to another set of soft tyres before needing intermediates when the rain came down increasingly heavily in the final 10 laps.

Norris said: "It was a very tough race - very, very tough. Not the best of launches off the line, but a lot of challenges today with the conditions and going on slicks in the wet is always tough.

"The main thing today was that I just kept it cool and I did not make any mistakes. I had the pace when I needed to so it was good. Nice to be back on the top step and what a place to do it as well."

Verstappen had made speedy progress up from his position at the back.

Initially, Lewis Hamilton, who had started alongside the Red Bull, progressed faster, and was ninth by lap two, but Verstappen soon got into his stride and passed the Ferrari within a further two laps and continued his forward progress.

By lap 10, Verstappen was up to a remarkable sixth place and right behind the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson, with Hadjar ahead chasing Russell, who by then was up to third after starting seventh.

But Russell dashed his own hopes when he stopped on lap 16, at the same time as Norris, and spun in the pit lane exit which mirrors on the inside of the track the run through the Senna S first two corners.

Russell was broadside in the pit lane as rivals squeezed past him left and right as he manoeuvred his way straight again and rejoined the race, now down in 10th.

After that, he drove well with strong pace to put himself back in contention and a fourth-place finish was a strong result in the circumstances.

He had more pace than Antonelli in the closing laps and the team ordered them to swap positions as they sealed their ninth constructors' title, and first since 2021.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was sixth, nowhere near Norris' pace, while Ferrari's Charles Leclerc took seventh after a topsy-turvy race ahead of Lawson and Hamilton.

After his initial burst up the field, the seven-time champion lacked pace, despite pushing correctly for an early stop for slicks, and could make no more ground.

Although leading Leclerc for much of the race, Hamilton fell behind him with his second stop for slicks, while Leclerc hung on for the change to intermediates to consolidate his position.

Audi's Nico Hulkenberg took the final point for 10th place.

The season is due to end with a final triple header, starting with the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The night race is due to start at 04:00 GMT on Sunday, 22 November.

title: Leclerc penalised for Lawson clash; Antonelli and Oliver Bearman also punished after F1 Brazilian GP
Norris brilliant in wet & Verstappen recovery extraordinary - driver ratings
text:
McLaren's Lando Norris secured his third win of the season on Sunday by beating Max Verstappen to victory at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Norris started on pole position but lost the lead of the wet-dry-wet race to new world champion Kimi Antonelli on the opening lap. But after an early pit stop for dry tyres, he regained control when Mercedes' Antonelli spun at the first corner.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his eighth consecutive podium with another eye-catching drive in tricky conditions at Interlagos, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar finished third.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Brazil.

Pretty difficult to ask for much more for the McLaren driver. Fastest in first practice on Friday, brilliant in the wet to take pole and then kept his head through constantly changing conditions to win comfortably. Losing the lead at the start was only a minor blemish.

Another extraordinary recovery drive in the Red Bull. Fastest in final practice and then charged from 21st to second, making up 10 places almost immediately, and once again looking completely at home in difficult conditions.

One of his strongest weekends all season. Qualified well, ran with team-mate Verstappen for much of the race and delivered another podium despite a few mistakes along the way. Had the pace to make Red Bull think before eventually letting Verstappen through.

The pace was excellent all weekend and second in qualifying showed what was possible, even if his engine penalty dropped him to seventh. Spinning his Mercedes on the pit exit was a huge error and probably cost him a podium, but recovering to fourth was a very strong response.

For the opening stint this looked like the perfect first race as world champion. A brilliant start and built a healthy lead, but spinning it away after switching to the slick tyres unlocked a messy afternoon.

Another weekend where things never really clicked. His qualifying result was compromised by the timing of the red flag, but he was a long way from Norris' pace in the race and finished almost a minute behind his McLaren team-mate.

An excellent weekend in the Racing Bulls. Qualified fifth, started third and even ran second during the opening stages before eventually slipping backwards as the race developed.

A very good recovery from 14th on the grid after his power-unit penalty. Qualified fourth on pure pace and worked his way through to eighth. He passed Lawson towards the end but was given a five-second penalty for hitting the New Zealander, which means he finishes behind him.

The opening few laps were vintage Hamilton as he charged from 20th to ninth, but the progress then stalled. He struggled for pace in the Ferrari on the intermediate tyres, and a late spin capped a race where more looked possible after such a promising start.

Outstanding in the wet qualifying session to put Audi sixth before penalties promoted him to fourth. A 10-second time penalty for going off track in his battle with Franco Colapinto hurt his Sunday, but he still came away with the final point.

Norris wins gripping race after Antonelli and Russell errors

Norris sparkles in Sao Paulo despite firework mishap

His qualifying was cut short by a mechanical problem in his Racing Bulls and further power-unit changes left him starting well down the order. Recovered well to 11th and came extremely close to points.

Reaching Q3 for the first time this season was a big positive and he raced well enough to even get ahead of Hamilton with a spectacular move in the Aston Martin. P12 doesn't look spectacular, but there was plenty to like about the weekend.

Alpine struggled badly in the wet qualifying session but Colapinto made a reasonable recovery. Finished ahead of team-mate Pierre Gasly and was involved in the battle with Hulkenberg that eventually earned the Audi driver a penalty.

A disappointing weekend after both Alpines went out in Q1. Made a little progress from 16th on the grid but finished behind Colapinto and never really threatened the points.

Saturday was the highlight after reaching Q3 for the first time this season and earning ninth on the grid. Unfortunately the race went the opposite way and he fell back to 15th in the Williams.

Showed good speed before qualifying but his crash in the Audi in Q1 put him on the back foot for his home race.

A really strong Saturday to put the Haas eighth in qualifying and sixth on the grid. The race was a completely different story, though, as he tumbled out of contention and eventually finished 17th.

Starting last because of his engine penalty made it difficult from the outset. Kept his nose clean, picked up several positions in his Cadillac and reached the finish ahead of a Williams and a Haas.

Unlucky to have his Q2 attempt interrupted by the red flag just as he switched to the intermediates, but Sunday offered little recovery.

Plenty of raw speed on his F1 debut in the Haas but plenty of learning too. Reaching Q2 in those conditions was impressive, although two qualifying incidents and a difficult race ultimately left him 20th.

Out in Q1 and never looked capable of matching Aston Martin team-mate Alonso across the weekend.

Only 20th in qualifying before being promoted a couple of places on the grid. His race was over before it had even begun, with Cadillac retiring his car with a technical problem, so Sunday itself is impossible to judge.

Fastest lap is not enough to overcome a slow start for Cameron Mason sixth at UEC European Cyclo-cross Championships
author: Lyne Lamoureux
text:
A slow start derailed Cameron Mason ’s quest to step back onto the podium in the elite men’s race at the UEC European Cyclo-cross Championships on Sunday. Starting on the second row, the British champion was in 27th place after Swiss rider Kevin Kuhn, who also started on the second row, took the holeshot and led the field onto the tough course in Zeddam, in the Netherlands.

One lap later, as the field was stretching out and gaps started to form, Mason was 17 seconds back, in 23rd position. Not giving up, the 26-year-old started to give chase, trying to pick his way through the riders on a technical course which offered limited spots to pass.

At the start of the sixth of nine laps, Mason had moved up to 10th place, at 21 seconds back. But at that point, three riders, including eventual winner Thibau Nys (Belgium) , had pulled away.

After putting a massive turn of speed on lap seven, Mason set the fastest lap of the race in 6:19, one second quicker than Nys. He then bridged across to a three-rider chase group, which was rapidly closing the gap and caught Kuhn on the penultimate lap.

With only two riders up front, the bronze medal was still at play. So Mason went to the front of the chase group, coming as close as seven seconds to the leading duo, but the other riders in the group could not or would not provide assistance, and the gap grew out.

By the start of the bell lap, the chase group was at 12 seconds and locked in battle for third place, which was ultimately taken by Niels Vandeputte (Belgian). Crossing the line in sixth place, Mason is still looking to equal or beat his second place in 2023 in Pontchâteau, France.

“I didn’t stop believing until one lap to go, when I threw it all away. Even after the shocking position I put myself in on the first part of the race, I wasn’t raised to be a quitter,” Mason wrote on social media .

“Today, like with the rest of life, I realised no one is going to do it for you. There will be many wonderful people who will help, guide and believe in you. But when it really matters, it’s all on you.”

“That’s why today hurts so much. To show just how much I wanted it, but to fall short of a result on paper. “But what a privilege it is to put my heart and soul into doing hard things. I will be back.”

title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
author: Associated Press
text:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo

Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. He said some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

title: ‘Why not?’ - Isaac Del Toro on a Mexican rider winning Tour de France in the future
author: Lyne Lamoureux
text:
Competing at the top level for the past two years, since his breakthrough at the 2024 Tour Down Under, Isaac del Toro has done more than win. He has also learned from both his successes and mistakes, something that he repeats in interviews, as he did on the eve of the Singapore Criterium.

The UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider enjoyed a remarkable 2026 season which included winning the overall at four WorldTour stage races: the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico, the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and the Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal. He also won a stage and finished third overall on his Tour de France debut, helping team leader Tadej Pogačar secure his fifth overall victory.

Speaking on media day ahead of the Singapore exhibition race, which he went on to win , Del Toro told he was “very happy” with his season.

“Happy to have had all the experiences this year and satisfied because I know I can apply them to the future to always do a little better. Obviously, with that emphasis on continuing to work hard.”

From racing his first WorldTour race in Australia for UAE Emirates XRG at just 20 years of age, Del Toro quickly matured into taking on the mantle of team leader two years later.

“It's something we tried to achieve from the moment I signed. We didn't know how quickly or slowly it would happen, or if it was even possible in such a competitive team where everyone is at a very high level,” Del Toro said.

His progression began at the Tour Down Under, but Del Toro initially preferred to delay taking on leadership responsibilities as long as possible so he could learn from those around him.

“After a year, I developed more and began to understand what kind of rider I am; I can handle myself well in quite a few situations, although I don't know if I specialise in anything.”

As only the second Mexican rider to win a Tour de France stage, following Raúl Alcalá's victories in 1989 and 1990, Del Toro understands the responsibility that he carries, though he admits to sometimes forgetting it “for a moment”.

“They remind you that you're a public figure, and you try to be measured. I know there's someone expecting something from me and trying to put me in the best possible light, so I take that as a responsibility.”

When asked if it could be possible for a Mexican rider to win the Tour de France in the future, Del Toro replied: “Why not?”

It wasn’t that long ago that the idea of having a Slovenian dominate racing would have raised eyebrows.

“If others have won it, why can't a Mexican? We have two legs, two arms, a head... I don't see it as distant or impossible. It's difficult, but I see the same possibilities as everyone else.”

“I won my first stage in Barcelona, I made the podium in the Giro, and I know I can be competitive. More athletes are coming up over the years; I'm not just referring to myself, but to the fact that, as Mexicans, of course it's possible.”

'The most ridiculous reaction I have ever heard' – Three-time world champion Sanne Cant blasts UCI jury over Marie Schreiber’s relegation
author: Owen Rogers
text:
After crossing the line first in the elite women’s race on Saturday , Schreiber was relegated to second place for an irregular sprint, the Luxembourg rider missing out on what would have been the biggest result of her career.

It was clear from the head-on coverage that she did make a move to her left, but despite eventual winner Lucinda Brand asserting she was not impeded, the race jury interpreted this as a breach serious enough to warrant the relegation.

Not only was Schreiber upset by the issue , but she has been joined by Cant, who has been part of the SD Worx team for two winters, and previously won three rainbow jerseys among 126 race wins during a long career.

"It is the most ridiculous reaction I have ever heard," Cant told after the race.

"I spent a very long time on a bike myself and I have never experienced anything like this. If we already find a mistake here... I think there are other sprints taking place on the road where nothing happens."

Brand did not file a complaint, according to her Dutch cycling federation.

"It really was the UCI president [of the commissaire's panel] who saw it, but it is anyone's guess what he saw," Cant said.

"Maybe he should try sprinting on a 'cross bike himself. It will never be straight. I think the track was wide enough to pass."

Schreiber did not attend the podium ceremony, which, according to reports in the Belgian press, was a decision that came primarily from Cant.

"I didn't want her to stand on [the podium]. That is not because there is no respect for Lucinda, but because you shouldn't accept a medal that doesn't belong to you," Cant told .

Cant added that "we are not going to leave it at this", and while it is unclear what action SD Worx-Protime might be able to take, given that the European Championships are contested by national teams, the Luxembourg cycling federation has announced it will appeal the decision.

title: European Cyclo-cross Championships: Thibau Nys wins second elite title as Belgium sweeps the podium
author: Lyne Lamoureux
text:
Thibau Nys powered away from his Belgian compatriot Joran Wyseure on the final lap on the slippery, heavy course to win his second elite men’s title at the UEC Cyclo-cross European Championships in Zeddam, Netherlands on Sunday.

Wyseure crossed the line seven seconds later to claim silver, bettering his third place from last year. Completing an all-Belgian podium. Niels Vandeputte took bronze, winning the sprint from a four-rider chase group.

With the largest squads in the race, Belgium fielding eight riders and the Netherlands five, the two teams took turns in the early laps, forcing the other to expend energy closing gaps on the slippery, heavy course. The tactical battle between the eternal rivals continued until Nys launched an attack on an off-camber section leading into the long stairs. Kuhn responded immediately, with Wyseure on his wheel.

Nys and Wyseure pulled away with three laps to go, and battled each other until Nys put in a big acceleration, opening up a gap on the stairs and holding it to the finish line.

“A tough one. I think it was a hard and a really nice battle with Joran. He was super strong and it was really difficult to get rid of each other, so I felt halfway through the race that it will be a big explosion in the last lap," Nys said.

Nys agreed that the course was demanding: “It is, I mean, it is quite hard, but on the other hand, it's quite difficult to make a gap. And especially when you have to pull in the front on the section on the road on the finish line, it takes away a lot of energy, and it was a bit of a gamble over there.”

“There is a lot more to come. For me, every race is just as important as another one, and next week is just as important as today’s the European Championships. So yeah, I will try to let the jersey shine.”

Zeddam already hosted the 2006 Cyclocross World Championships, won by Erwin Vervecken (Belgium) and Marianne Vos (Netherlands).

34 riders, staged across five rows, took on the updated 2.97 km course, designed by the same Vervecken. The toughest obstacle was the revamped staircase with its 99 steps, used for the first time in a championship course. Also new was a 60-meter-long rider bridge alongside the Grafelijke Korenmolen, the oldest still-operating windmill in the Netherlands.

Kevin Kuhn (Switzerland) took the holeshot, surging from the second row on the long, slightly uphill start straight, and led the pack on the first lap. Spain’s Felipe Orts took over setting the pace on the second lap, while Cameron Mason (Great Britain), after a slow start, was 22 seconds back.

The tactical battle ended when Belgian Thibau Nys launched an attack on an off-camber section leading into the stairs. Kuhn responded immediately, with Belgian Joran Wyseure on his wheel, getting a free ride.

By the start of the fourth lap, Nys had four seconds on Kuhn and Wyseure, and then 14 seconds on the second chase group, which organised behind Ryan Kamp (Netherlands). Once a gap was established to the group behind, Wyseure came to the front and reeled in his compatriot. Behind, Joris Nieuwenhuis (Netherlands), with Belgian duo Michael Vanthourenhout and Niels Vandeputte close by, launched from the chase group.

Nys continued to apply pressure, as Kuhn fell off the pace, while Wyseure worked hard to get back on by the start of the seventh lap. Kuhn, 10 seconds back, was caught on the stairs by Orts, Vandeputte, Nieuwenhuis and Mason, leading to a five-way battle for the bronze medal.

Coming into the ninth and final lap, Nys ooked behind him across the 12-second gap at the chasing group, before putting a big acceleration to drop Wyseure. He built on a slight gap opened on the stairs, to power on to take the win.

title: Singapore Criterium: Isaac Del Toro takes surprise solo win as the sprinters miss out
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Isaac del Toro continued his battle with rival Paul Seixas on Sunday, the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider taking a surprise solo win in the Singapore Criterium.

Both he and Seixas (Decathlon-CMA CGM) had been part of a four-man group which escaped the bunch on the 23rd lap around the city. As the final lap approached, the Mexican champion simply rode off the front of that group, holding Seixas a few seconds behind him until the line.

Seixas hung on for second place, a handful of seconds behind, with Søren Warenskjold (UNO X Mobility) winning the sprint for third place. The peloton crossed the line some 30 seconds behind.

With the traditional Saitama Criterium in Japan coming next weekend, Singapore was the first of two Far Eastern criteriums arranged by the Tour de France organisers, ASO, with the race taking place over 25 laps of a two-kilometre city circuit. The race started aggressively and remained that way throughout, with multiple breakaways going clear all day long.

The first of those got away after the opening intermediate sprint and contained Baptiste Viestroffer (Lotto-Intermarché), Patrick Konrad (Lidl-Trek), home road champion Eamon Lim (CCACHE-BODYWRAP) and Rasmus Søjberg Pedersen (Decathlon-CMA CGM). They were away for a handful of laps, but the intermediate sprints, which came every five laps, dictated the race, the peloton re-forming before each one.

That meant that none of the breakaways, however large, were able to gain any kind of advantage, with 10 seconds being all most would create.

Biniam Girmay won the first intermediate sprint, and his NSN team were instrumental in containing the breakaways’ ambitions. Even a strong group of six was unable to build a lead as the race approached the final kick, with five laps of the race to go.

One lap after that final sprint, French sensation Seixas let an all-star group of four up the road, with Del Toro, Mauro Schmid (Jayco-AlUla) and Søren Waerenskjold (UNO X Mobility) quickly establishing a lead and taking 10 seconds into the final three laps. With little conviction in the chase, their lead expanded and, at the start of the penultimate lap, that advantage was out to 30 seconds, the greatest advantage of any of the day’s breaks, and the race seemed set to end with a four-up sprint.

title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
text:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester .

See My World , a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations .

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

title: The wet-weather challenges thrown up by Brazilian GP qualifying
'It’s disrespectful to steal the biggest moment of my career' - Marie Schreiber condemns Euro cyclo-cross relegation
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Schreiber crossed the line first in the Elite Women’s race at Zeddam in the Netherlands, apparently bagging the biggest win of her career, but a few minutes later, she was relegated for an irregular sprint. She later refused to attend the podium ceremony.

"The UCI and UEC they always advocate for and everyone they always advocate for clean and fair sport and then they do this, it’s unfair," Schreiber said after the race.

She and World Champion Lucinda Brand (Netherlands) had come into the finish straight together after the Luxembourgish rider overtook on the brutal run up the flight of 99 steps. Leading out, Schreiber opened her sprint early, holding Brand at bay. From the footage, it was clear she did move to her left as the pair closed in on the finish line, and it seems it was this move the race commissaires penalised.

"We reviewed the footage and both me and Lucinda said our views," Schreiber said. "Lucinda said I did nothing wrong, she couldn’t have passed anyway, so I think it’s really thankful that she said this, but it doesn’t change the commissaires’ decision.

"It’s a sprint after 50 minutes of all out racing, you come with 190 heart rate, I change my gear, I saw I moved a little bit to the left, but then I think if every person watches the race you know this moving around it’s normal. I did not close the door on purpose or anything, Lucinda knows this and she also said it.

"I think it’s disrespectful to steal the biggest moment of my career just for this because I think for being fair everyone knows I won, if it would have been decided by two centimetres I can argue with them I can understand, but like this I think it’s just disrespectful to be honest."

Though Schreiber was relegated to second place, with Brand’s compatriot Ceylon del Carmen Alvarado in third, she was not present on the podium, and was asked if her team manager, former World Champion Sanne Can’t, had advised her not to attend, something which may mean she is fined by the race jury.

"Yeah, I was going to go because I thought everyone’s going to hate me if I don’t go, but then it’s like if they’re being like this to me then I also don’t owe them anything, to be honest. It’s hard to be standing here right now, so you can imagine it’s harder to stand on the podium, so they said I shouldn’t go, I shouldn’t let myself be treated like this. I can live with a fine probably better than going to sleep tonight."

Though she has a World Cup race win to her name, victory in the Euros would have been by far the biggest success of Schreiber’s career. Riding for her road trade team, SD Worx-Protime, Schreiber has had an excellent start to the 2026/27 season, winning the two opening races of the year, taking three more wins, with third place at the X2O Koppenbergcross her worst result.

title: Supercars Sandown: Payne Sunday win sets up title challenge
Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm
author: Rebecca Ratcliffe, Gloria Dickie and Elisângela Mendonça
text:
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo .

A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize , which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild .

Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.

Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.

This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.

The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.

Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.

“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”

Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.

Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.

“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.

Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.

A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.

Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.

“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.

Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”

Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.

The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.

Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.

“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.
